RAUL ARIANO/BLOOMBERG NEWS   Something curious is happening in China. Young people, college-educated and burned out, are picking up Mao Zedong’s early writings. They’re reading the founding father of the People’s Republic not as nostalgia, but the way an earlier American generation might have read Studs Terkel: as someone who gave language to why the system grinds people down.

   For decades, the Chinese state has had a deal with the people. Work hard, buy an apartment, climb the economic ladder and stay out of politics. Now, for tens of millions of young Chinese, that deal is off. The apartments are worth less than their parents paid. The ladder leads to a grueling work schedule and a work title that doesn’t cover rent. That’s the backdrop against which young Chinese today reach for Mao’s thoughts on how the powerful exploit the working class, using them to make sense of their lives in 2026.

   The phenomenon speaks to how much the country’s decadeslong economic bargain has broken.

   But what actually broke? That’s the question at the center of a new International Monetary Fund book, “Toward a New Economic Growth Model for China,” co-written by Krishna Srinivasan, the fund’s top Asia official. I spoke with him ahead of the book’s launch last month, and his diagnosis is blunt: China’s growth model has “largely run its course.”

   The symptoms are everywhere, from the collapse of a massive housing market to a plunge in consumer confidence. They are not, by themselves, an explanation for the Mao revival. But they help explain the sense of economic disillusionment that has made his old critique newly resonant. 

   In Chengdu, a second-tier city in China’s southwest that was once a magnet for young professionals, secondary-market property prices have fallen at least 15% since their peak in 2023, Srinivasan said. In Guangdong, China’s export powerhouse, he noted, retail sales dropped about 3% last year. People have paid for apartments that were never delivered. Household wealth has evaporated, and with it, confidence. “What is holding consumption back,” Srinivasan said, “is that confidence is low.”

   Making it safe to save less.   The IMF’s prescription sounds simple enough: China needs its people to spend more and save less. But as anyone who has lived in the country knows, families aren’t hoarding cash out of some cultural quirk. They’re saving because a hospital bill could wipe them out, rural pensions are a pittance and migrant workers in cities still can’t access urban social-safety nets.

   “You can’t just wish for people to consume more,” Srinivasan said. The state has to build the healthcare, pension and unemployment systems that make it safe to save less. Trust, he said, is “central,” and right now it operates through institutions that aren’t delivering.

     Krishna Srinivasan KENT NISHIMURA/AFP/GETTY IMAGES   There’s an external dimension to all of this. China’s weak domestic demand not only hurts its own economy. The country has built huge productive capacity, but people aren’t buying enough to absorb it. So factories look abroad. The resulting competition at home keeps prices low, making Chinese goods cheaper abroad and encouraging even more exports to flood the world .

   The export surge, Srinivasan said, is “the external manifestation of unresolved domestic imbalances.” 

   In other words, the trade tensions roiling Washington, Brussels and elsewhere aren’t separate from the broken apartment in Chengdu or the burned-out graduate reading Mao in Shenzhen.

   Between 2019 and 2025, trade restrictions globally tripled, Srinivasan noted. And here is an interesting argument: if the rest of the world won’t buy what China produces, then the old model of investing more, building more and exporting the surplus simply stops working. “It’s an incentive” for China to change its model, he said, “whether it’s from outside or from inside.”

   The IMF book calls on Beijing to overhaul incentives, from growth targets that drive local officials to chase GDP at any cost to a fiscal system that leaves provinces dependent on land sales and industrial policies that favor producers over consumers.

   So what happens if Beijing doesn’t act? I asked Srinivasan to paint the scenario that worries him most. “A prolonged slowdown with weak domestic demand and deflation,” he said. “The longer you wait, the bigger the problem becomes.”

   He calls his preferred outcome a “divine coincidence”: the reforms that would rescue China’s own consumers from stagnation are the same ones that would ease the trade tensions keeping the rest of the world up at night. 

   It’s a hopeful framing. Whether Beijing can move in that direction is a different question. Meanwhile, the Mao reading groups will likely keep growing.

   Do you think external pressure—tariffs and other trade restrictions—will actually force Beijing to reform, or will it just entrench the current model ? Write to me at lingling.wei@wsj.com . Include your full name and location, and I might publish your response in an upcoming issue (if you’re reading this in your inbox, you can just hit reply).

China in a Few Headlines

 

• Exclusive: Chinese officials made unusual demands for the U.S. to accommodate Xi Jinping’s need for rest during a summit with President Trump.

 

• Germany and France are proposing a new weapon for Europe to fight back against a flood of cheap Chinese imports, setting the stage for a confrontation with Beijing.

 

• China is promoting a sanitized, state-approved version of Tibetan culture for Han tourists as Beijing prepares for a looming struggle over Tibetan Buddhism.

 

• Dozens of Iranian or Iranian-linked tankers that had participated in the shadowy trade of getting sanctioned oil to China have been stuck in the waters near Asian countries.

 
 
 

The Number

 
1/3
 

That’s the percentage China makes up of global foldable smartphone sales, according to research firm Counterpoint Research. That suggests an opportunity for Apple’s new iPhone Duo—if it can overcome competition from Chinese brands.

 
 
 

A Closer Look

 
 
 

The Trump administration is engaged in a multibillion-dollar, governmentwide effort to loosen Beijing’s chokehold on critical minerals. It is slowly starting to work.

 

Reader Responses

 

Last week, we asked what you think about the role of Peng Liyuan, Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s wife, and her evolution. Readers shared their thoughts: Readers shared their thoughts:

 

“Peng Liyuan made a strong impression by speaking English with first lady Trump without needing an interpreter. She presents China as confident, open to the world, and easy to relate to. This approach quietly signals equality, not a student-teacher relationship. Her English skills are praised abroad, but talk about her language abilities and fashion is closely managed on Chinese platforms.”—Luis Reyes, Massachusetts

 

“Peng Liyuan’s influence extends beyond the PLA. She heads the so-called Shandong Clique, a faction comprising senior administrators, military figures and officials who share ties to Peng’s home province of Shandong or have advanced through her professional and personal network.”—David Chu, Connecticut

 

“Xi Jinping gripping his wife’s hand down the stairs in Washington was more than a display of physical caution; it was a vivid symbol of a regime regressing into court politics, where an isolated ruler trusts marriage over hollowed-out party institutions.”—Shinya Hanamura, Japan

 

“In monarchical or authoritarian governments, the issue of succession is of critical importance. Since China is not a monarchy but has an authoritarian structure (some may argue totalitarian), succession planning doesn’t follow a hereditary path but is decided within the party apparatus with limited visibility to the outside world. In such structures, the life partner of the current leader may find themselves in a precarious position.”—Eugene P. Grace, Pennsylvania

 

(Responses have been condensed and edited.)

 
 
 

A Name in the News

 
 
Cathy Sparks, the head of Nike’s China business.
 

Cathy Sparks’ first job at Nike was selling sneakers in an Oregon store. Thirty years later, she’s in charge of leading the company’s turnaround in China, its second-largest market. It is a daunting challenge for her, as Nike’s revenue in China and Taiwan is down nearly 30% from its peak five years ago.
